title: Vouchsafe
pitch: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation.
about_excerpt: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation. Like Comment Story Updates The problem To rent a flat in Britain you upload your payslips, your bank statements and your passport to six letting agents. Every one of them keeps a copy, forever. None of them wanted your salary. They wanted one answer: does your income cover three times the rent, yes or no. That gap between what is asked for and what is needed is the whole product. What Vouchsafe is Two origins. Your file lives on one; a letting agency lives on the other. Your facts never leave your browser. The agency asks a question through WebMCP and gets one word back. The interesting part is what happens when you change your mind. Withdraw a permission and the tool is not disabled on the agency's side, it is deregistered . Authority here is not a permission check. It is whether the tool exists. A withheld permission is not a guarded tool that refuses; there is no tool, so it cannot be called, guessed at, or talked into existence by anything written into a page or a prompt. How it is built Vanilla ES modules. No build step, no framework, no runtime dependencies, and zero third-party requests from either origin, which is enforced by a test rather than asserted in a README. The cross-origin round trip is the part we could not find anyone else doing in full: Your file registers each allowed question with exposedTo naming the agency's origin. The agency calls getTools({fromOrigins}) and discovers them. It re-registers each discovered tool as a local tool, so an agent sees one flat toolset and never has to know two websites were involved. On toolchange , it diffs and tears down proxies for anything that has stopped being offered. Step 3 and step 4 are what make revocation land mid-conversation. Things we found out about Chrome's implementation We wrote these down with reproduction steps because we could not find them documented anywhere. getTools() hands back inputSchema as a JSON string , but registerTool() demands an object . Re-registering a discovered tool fails silently until you parse it. getTools({fromOrigins}) also returns your own tools, so a naive proxy loop registers proxies for its own proxies. A cross-origin iframe's tools do not appear in the host's plain getTools() . You have to ask for them by origin. Federation is scoped to the frame tree, not the browser. toolchange fires once per registration, not once per batch, so a nine permission grant is nine events and the handler has to be idempotent. Revocation crosses the origin boundary with no channel of our own. The browser does it. The declarative form API derives the schema from the form's own inputs. We get sixteen parameters for free, and omitting toolautosubmit parks the call for a human, which is a consent gate written in HTML. The hard part, and the honest limit A yes-or-no predicate leaks more than one bit if the caller picks the threshold. Ask "is income at least 3x £2000", then £1500, then £1300, and five calls have bracketed a salary to a £3,600 window. Every individual answer is legitimate. The sequence is a salary disclosure wearing a predicate's clothes. So your file tracks the bracket each origin has established, prices what has been learned in bits, and stops answering once the remaining uncertainty falls below a floor. In the demo you watch five numbers get answered and the sixth refused. We are not claiming this is leak-proof. A patient caller spread across sessions, or several origins pooling answers, defeats a per-origin window. Adding noise would bound it properly and would also make an affordability check occasionally wrong, which is not a trade a letting decision can absorb. This is the cheap honest version, and it says so in the code. What we learned about testing this Playwright was the wrong tool and we can say exactly why: its launcher appends its own --enable-features flag after ours, so WebMCP is silently dropped and the API is simply absent. We drive Chrome and Brave over the DevTools Protocol directly instead, and the same suite runs against both. Two bugs worth confessing. Two new modules were written and never deployed, so a 404 killed the whole module graph and both live pages rendered blank while 108 tests passed, because every one of them ran against a local server where the files existed. And an announcer banner marked hidden painted on every page load anyway, because display: grid on the element beats the user agent's display: none for [hidden] . Both now have tests. 118 tests: 66 unit, 52 in a real browser. Verify it yourself Do not take any of this on trust. /proof.html reads the browser's own tool registry on both origins and redraws on toolchange . It registers nothing itself, which is what makes it a witness rather than a participant. Toggle a permission and watch a tool stop existing. video_transcript_excerpt: To rent a flat in Britain, you upload your pay slips, your bank statements, and your passport to six letting agents. They keep them forever. None of them wanted your salary. They wanted one answer. Does your income cover three times the rent? Yes or no? This is Vouch Safe. Your facts stay on your own origin in your own browser, and nothing on this page can send them anywhere. Right now, this letting agency knows nothing at all about you. Watch the diagram. You allow nine questions in your own file. Each one is a question they may ask, not a document they may keep. Those nine questions just became answerable across the boundary between two different websites. Your file offer them. The agency asked for them. There is no server in between. Now the agency runs its checks. Nine questions and nine one-word answers. You qualify. >> And this site still holds nothing about you. Now suppose the agency gets greedy and starts guessing your salary by moving the threshold it asks about. >> Every one of those answers was legitimate on its own. >> The run of them is not. Your file noticed, and it stopped answering. >> Change your mind, and the question stops being answerable. >> Nothing is asked to cooperate. The tool simply stops existing on their side. >> Gone in the middle of the conversation. >> That check can no longer run. Authority here is not a permission check. It is whether the tool exists. This page reads the browser's own registry and registers nothing itself. The letting agent gets an answer. >> Not your life.

live_observation.first_impression: A letting-agent page lists available properties and check buttons beside them, alongside an embedded Vouchsafe file with granular permission controls and withdraw-all.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked Check again for Studio, Talbot Road.
live_observation.after_state: The page remained on the property/application view; no obvious visible result change was exposed in the snapshot.
live_observation.notes: The browser-side file permissions and one-word affordability concept are represented directly, including Allow controls and Withdraw everything.
